analysis.one_liner: Requires index and passive fund managers to pass corporate shareholder votes through to the fund's investors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2022 and referred to committee, but never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, when you own a company through an index fund in your 401(k), the fund's manager — firms like BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street — votes your shares in corporate elections. This bill would require those managers, when they control more than 1% of a company's votes, to ask each fund investor how to vote on major decisions like director elections and mergers, and to vote only the shares they actually received instructions on. It would keep fund managers voting on routine items. The bill never got a hearing or vote in the House Financial Services Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary savers whose retirement money sits in index and other passively managed funds would get to vote corporate shares themselves on big decisions — director elections, mergers, and sales of the company — instead of a fund manager voting for them. Corporate shareholders who currently face large blocs voted by a handful of asset managers would face a more scattered electorate.

how_it_helps.text: Investment advisers to passively managed funds that control more than 1% of a company's voting power must vote proportionate amounts of shares according to instructions from the fund's investors, and cannot vote shares for which no instructions were received.
Investors must be sent the proxy statement, annual report, and a form for returning voting instructions, with at least 5 business days to respond, and materials may be delivered electronically.
Advisers retain control over routine matters and get a safe harbor from legal liability if they choose not to solicit instructions on other matters, limiting the disruption to normal fund operations.

analysis.who_pays: The largest index fund managers would give up their concentrated power to vote huge blocs of corporate shares, and would bear the cost and logistics of soliciting and processing instructions from millions of individual fund holders. Companies would face shareholder votes decided by a much smaller and less predictable share of their investor base, and critics argue that would weaken informed oversight of corporate boards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large index fund managers and their staffs

drawbacks.text: Participation is the weak point: most small investors historically do not return proxy ballots, so pass-through voting could leave major corporate decisions decided by a small, self-selected slice of holders while coordinated, informed engagement by fund managers disappears — a risk an honest supporter of investor democracy has to weigh.

Advisers would have to send proxy materials to every voting person and cover the expense of soliciting and tabulating millions of instructions; the bill allows passively managed funds themselves to pay those direct and indirect costs, which are ultimately borne by fund investors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's goal — giving the actual owners of corporate America a say in who runs it — is genuine and responds to real concern about a few asset managers voting trillions of dollars. But the design's success depends entirely on whether small investors actually vote; if they mostly do not, the practical result could be less accountability for corporate management, not more. The exemptions for routine matters and the adviser safe harbor soften the burden, but costs of mass solicitation would fall on funds and their investors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2022 and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 27, 2022, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was taken during the remainder of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023.
The bill attracted only two Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support in the record, giving it little momentum to reach the committee agenda.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest index fund managers keep their power to vote enormous blocs of corporate shares on behalf of fund investors, and nothing changes for corporate boards, which face the same shareholder electorate as before.

industries.industry: Large index and passive fund managers (e.g., BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street)
industries.note: They would lose their concentrated power to vote massive blocs of corporate shares — power they exercise over companies held in ordinary people's retirement accounts. They argue that power lets them press companies on governance and long-term value; the bill would hand those votes back to individual savers.

If the giant fund managers can no longer vote as unified blocs and most small holders skip the ballot, management-backed directors and proposals would face less coordinated shareholder scrutiny — the opposite of what everyday shareholders as a group want from governance.

industries.industry: Proxy distribution and fund administration services
industries.note: Soliciting and tabulating instructions from millions of fund holders would create large new demand for the firms that deliver proxy materials and process investor votes.
